items.title: Deep Learning the Indus Script
items.note: Presents a neural pipeline that segments photographs of inscribed objects and outputs grapheme strings, a step toward reproducible corpus building.

items.title: The Indus Script and Economics: A Role for Indus Seals and Tablets in Rationing and Administration of Labor
items.note: One of the 2009 entropy authors proposes an administrative reading of seals and tablets as records of rations and labour, without phonetic values.

items.title: Interrogating Indus inscriptions to unravel their mechanisms of meaning conveyance
items.note: Argues from co-occurrence, collocation and positional patterns that seals and tablets were formalised data-carriers, like proto-cuneiform tablets, mixing document and linguistic syntax.

items.title: A method of identifying allographs in undeciphered scripts and its application to the Indus Valley Script
items.who: S. Daggumati and P. Z. Revesz
items.note: Uses sign positions to show that many mirrored signs are directional variants, implying a smaller sign list and affecting entropy-based comparisons.

items.title: Linguistic Hegemony and Latent Typology: The Case of Harappan Script Scholarship
items.note: Historiographical critique arguing that the field has been dominated by the assumption that the signs encode language, and tracing its causes.

items.title: A Catalog of Indus Signs
items.note: Published sign catalogue from the ICIT project, giving a documented sign list and variants against which corpus statistics can be checked.

items.title: Semantic scope of Indus inscriptions comprising taxation, trade and craft licensing, commodity control and access control: archaeological and script-internal evidence
items.note: Argues the inscriptions encode no proper names and served semasiographic or logographic administrative functions, a middle position between full writing and emblem.

items.title: Tamil Nadu offers US$1 million prize for Indus script decipherment
items.note: Announced with a state archaeology study comparing about 15,000 graffiti-marked sherds from Tamil Nadu sites with Indus signs; the prize presumes a decipherable script.

items.title: How Non-Linguistic Is the Indus Sign System? A Synthetic-Baseline Scorecard
items.note: Scores 1,916 deduplicated inscriptions against synthetic heraldic and administrative baselines and finds the corpus matches neither cleanly.

items.title: On the Non-Specificity of Statistical Measures Used in Script Decipherment
items.note: Builds a synthetic emblem system with no phonology and, using a pre-compiled registry of 54 methods, finds it classed with the Indus corpus on every reproducible test.
